learn.hook: The iron in Delhi's Mehrauli pillar, the copper in your house wiring and the zinc on a galvanised bucket all sit in the same block of the periodic table, yet zinc is not called a transition metal. Why?
points: The d-block occupies groups 3–12, where d orbitals are progressively filled. It has four transition series: 3d (Sc to Zn), 4d (Y to Cd), 5d (La and Hf to Hg) and 6d (Ac and Rf to Cn).
The f-block (placed separately at the bottom) has two series: lanthanoids (4f, Ce to Lu) and actinoids (5f, Th to Lr).

A transition element has an incompletely filled d subshell in its ground state or in any of its common oxidation states. Zn, Cd and Hg have full d¹⁰ configurations in the ground state and in their common oxidation states, so they are not regarded as transition elements (though they are studied with them).
General configuration: (n−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns¹⁻²; Pd is an exception with 4d¹⁰ 5s⁰.
Exceptions in the 3d series due to the extra stability of half-filled and fully filled d orbitals: Cr = [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ (not 3d⁴ 4s²) and Cu = [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ (not 3d⁹ 4s²).

example.q: Copper has a full 3d¹⁰ subshell in its ground state. Why is it still called a transition element?
steps: Cu ground state: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹
Its common ion Cu²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁹
3d⁹ is incompletely filled in a common oxidation state
example.answer: Because Cu²⁺ (3d⁹) has an incomplete d subshell

learn.reallife: India's Hindustan Zinc and the stainless-steel industry of Jindal both work with d-block metals; nickel and chromium make the steel in your kitchen 'stainless'.

quiz.q: What is the ground-state electronic configuration of chromium (Z = 24)?
quiz.explain: A half-filled 3d⁵ subshell is extra stable, so one 4s electron moves into 3d.
steps: Expected Cr (Z = 24): [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s².
A half-filled 3d⁵ is extra stable, so one 4s electron moves to 3d: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹.
Answer: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹
quiz.mistake: Applies the simple filling order without the half-filled exception

quiz.q: Why are Zn, Cd and Hg not regarded as transition elements?
options: They have incompletely filled d orbitals
They have completely filled d¹⁰ orbitals in the ground state and in their common oxidation states
quiz.explain: Zn²⁺, Cd²⁺ and Hg²⁺ are all d¹⁰, so these elements never have a partly filled d subshell in common states.
steps: A transition element needs an incomplete d subshell in the ground state or a common oxidation state.
Zn, Cd, Hg and their M²⁺ ions are all d¹⁰, so they never qualify.
Answer: They have completely filled d¹⁰ orbitals in the ground state and in their common oxidation states
quiz.mistake: Thinks they lack d electrons

quiz.q: Which series of transition elements starts with lanthanum?
quiz.explain: La and then Hf to Hg make up the 5d series.
steps: 3d: Sc–Zn; 4d: Y–Cd; 5d: La, Hf–Hg; 6d: Ac, Rf–Cn.
So the series that starts with lanthanum is the 5d series.
Answer: The 5d series
quiz.mistake: Confuses La with the start of the 4f lanthanoid series

quiz.q: What is the general outer electronic configuration of the d-block elements?
quiz.explain: The d orbitals of the penultimate shell, (n−1)d, are being filled.
steps: In d-block elements the penultimate (n−1)d orbitals fill.
General configuration: (n−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns¹⁻².
Answer: (n−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns¹⁻²
quiz.mistake: Writes the d subshell in the same shell as s

quiz.q: How many unpaired electrons are present in Cu²⁺ (Z of Cu = 29)?
quiz.explain: Cu²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁹, which has one unpaired electron.
quiz.mistake: Removes electrons from 3d before 4s
steps: Cu: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹
Cu²⁺: remove 4s¹ and one 3d → 3d⁹
3d⁹ has 1 unpaired electron
Answer: 1

quiz.q: Which element of the d-block has the configuration 4d¹⁰ 5s⁰?
quiz.explain: Pd is the notable exception with an empty 5s orbital.
steps: Pd is the exception with an empty 5s orbital.
Pd = [Kr] 4d¹⁰ 5s⁰.
Answer: Palladium
quiz.mistake: Assumes every d-block element has at least one ns electron

quiz.q: Silver has the configuration [Kr] 4d¹⁰ 5s¹. Why is it considered a transition element?
options: In its +2 oxidation state it has an incomplete 4d⁹ subshell
Its ground state has an incomplete d subshell
quiz.explain: Ag²⁺ (4d⁹) has an incompletely filled d subshell, satisfying the definition.
steps: Ag ground state is 4d¹⁰ 5s¹ (full d subshell).
In Ag²⁺ it is 4d⁹, incomplete, so silver counts as a transition element.
Answer: In its +2 oxidation state it has an incomplete 4d⁹ subshell
quiz.mistake: Looks only at the ground state

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Copper has the configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ rather than [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s². Reason (R): A completely filled d subshell has extra stability.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Moving one electron from 4s to 3d gives the more stable full 3d¹⁰ subshell.
steps: A: Cu is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹, not 3d⁹ 4s². True.
R: a completely filled d subshell has extra stability. True.
Moving one 4s electron gives stable 3d¹⁰, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not link the exception to filled-subshell stability

teach.ask: Gappu pecks at zinc: 'Zinc is in the d-block, so why isn't it a transition element?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Transition elements need a partly filled d subshell in the atom or a common ion; Zn is always d¹⁰!
teach.nudge: What kind of d subshell defines a transition element, and what does zinc have?

revise.summary: The d-block (groups 3–12) has four transition series: 3d, 4d, 5d and 6d; the f-block has lanthanoids and actinoids. A transition element has an incomplete d subshell in its ground state or a common oxidation state, so Zn, Cd and Hg are excluded. General configuration (n−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns¹⁻².
focus: General configuration and exceptions (Cr, Cu, Pd)
Why Zn, Cd, Hg are not transition elements
remember: Cu²⁺ (3d⁹) and Ag²⁺ (4d⁹) have incomplete d subshells
traps: Don't write Cr as 3d⁴ 4s²
Don't call zinc a transition element

topics.title: Physical properties, atomic sizes and ionisation enthalpies

learn.hook: Tungsten in an old filament bulb stays solid above 3600 K, while mercury in a thermometer is liquid at room temperature. Both are d-block metals.
points: Transition elements are typically hard, lustrous metals with high melting and boiling points, high densities and high enthalpies of atomisation, due to strong metallic bonding that involves (n−1)d as well as ns electrons. Melting points rise to a maximum around the middle (d⁵) of each series, apart from anomalous values for Mn and Tc.
Zn, Cd and Hg have no unpaired d electrons, weaker metallic bonding, and hence low melting points; Hg is a liquid.

Across a series, atomic radius decreases at first and then becomes nearly constant because each added d electron shields the outer electrons poorly while nuclear charge increases. Density increases from Ti to Cu.

4d and 5d elements of the same group have almost identical radii (Zr 160 pm, Hf 159 pm) because of lanthanoid contraction: the poorly shielding 4f electrons filled before the 5d series pull the 5d atoms in.

Ionisation enthalpy rises across a series but irregularly. The second ionisation enthalpies of Cr and Cu are unusually high (removing an electron from stable d⁵ and d¹⁰ ions), and the third ionisation enthalpies of Mn (Mn²⁺ is d⁵) and Zn (Zn²⁺ is d¹⁰) are high.

example.q: Explain why Zr and Hf have almost the same atomic radius even though Hf has 32 more electrons.
steps: Between Zr (4d) and Hf (5d) come the 14 lanthanoids, filling 4f
4f electrons shield the nuclear charge poorly
Effective nuclear charge rises, cancelling the expected increase in size: lanthanoid contraction
example.answer: Lanthanoid contraction makes their radii nearly equal (160 pm and 159 pm)

learn.reallife: Zr and Hf are so alike that separating them for India's nuclear reactors (zirconium alloy tubes must be nearly hafnium-free) is a specialised job done at the Nuclear Fuel Complex, Hyderabad.

quiz.q: Why do transition metals have high melting points and enthalpies of atomisation?
options: Strong metallic bonding involving both (n−1)d and ns electrons
They have only s electrons for bonding
quiz.explain: Unpaired d electrons add to metallic bonding, which is strongest around the middle of a series.
steps: Transition metals have unpaired (n−1)d electrons besides ns electrons.
Both take part in strong metallic bonding, giving high melting points and enthalpies of atomisation.
Answer: Strong metallic bonding involving both (n−1)d and ns electrons
quiz.mistake: Thinks only ns electrons take part in metallic bonding

quiz.q: Which 3d metal has the lowest melting point?
quiz.explain: Zinc has a full 3d¹⁰ subshell and no unpaired d electrons, so its metallic bonding is weakest.
steps: Zinc has a full 3d¹⁰ subshell and no unpaired d electrons.
Its metallic bonding is weakest, so its melting point is lowest.
Answer: Zinc
quiz.mistake: Picks a metal from the middle of the series

quiz.q: Why are the atomic radii of Zr (160 pm) and Hf (159 pm) almost equal?
options: Hf has fewer electrons than Zr
quiz.explain: The poorly shielding 4f electrons filled before Hf cause a contraction that cancels the expected size increase.
steps: The 14 lanthanoids (4f filling) come between Zr and Hf.
Poor shielding by 4f electrons causes lanthanoid contraction, cancelling the expected size increase.
Answer: Lanthanoid contraction
quiz.mistake: Credits actinoid contraction, which affects later elements

quiz.q: Why is the second ionisation enthalpy of chromium unusually high?
options: Removing the second electron breaks the stable 3d⁵ configuration of Cr⁺
Chromium has a very large atomic radius
quiz.explain: Cr⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵, a stable half-filled subshell; removing another electron needs extra energy.
steps: Cr⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵, a stable half-filled subshell.
Removing a second electron breaks it, so the second ionisation enthalpy is high.
Answer: Removing the second electron breaks the stable 3d⁵ configuration of Cr⁺
quiz.mistake: Writes the wrong configuration for Cr⁺

quiz.q: Why is the third ionisation enthalpy of manganese unusually high?
options: Mn²⁺ has a stable half-filled 3d⁵ configuration
quiz.explain: Removing a third electron from Mn²⁺ (3d⁵) destroys the extra-stable half-filled subshell.
steps: Mn²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵, half-filled and stable.
Removing a third electron destroys this, so the third ionisation enthalpy is high.
Answer: Mn²⁺ has a stable half-filled 3d⁵ configuration
quiz.mistake: Confuses half-filled with fully filled

quiz.q: How does atomic radius generally change across the 3d series?
options: It decreases sharply all the way
It decreases at first and then becomes nearly constant
quiz.explain: Increasing nuclear charge contracts the atom, but poor shielding by d electrons soon balances the effect.
steps: Nuclear charge rises across the series and pulls electrons in.
Poor shielding by added d electrons soon balances it, so radius decreases then stays nearly constant.
Answer: It decreases at first and then becomes nearly constant
quiz.mistake: Assumes the trend is as steep as in s- and p-block

quiz.q: Which property increases from titanium to copper in the 3d series?
quiz.explain: Atoms get slightly smaller while atomic mass increases, so density rises from Ti to Cu.
steps: From Ti to Cu atoms get slightly smaller while atomic mass increases.
So density increases.
Answer: Density
quiz.mistake: Assumes size also increases

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Mercury is a liquid at room temperature. Reason (R): Mercury has no unpaired d electrons, so its metallic bonding is weak.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: With a full 5d¹⁰ 6s² configuration, Hg has weak metallic bonding and a very low melting point.
steps: A: mercury is liquid at room temperature. True.
R: Hg has no unpaired d electrons, so metallic bonding is weak. True.
Weak bonding gives a very low melting point, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not link unpaired electrons to metallic bond strength

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is lanthanoid contraction, and why do zirconium and hafnium look like twins?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Poor shielding by 4f electrons shrinks the 5d atoms, so Zr and Hf end up nearly the same size!
teach.nudge: You named it. Which electrons cause it, and what do they fail to do?

revise.summary: Transition metals are hard and dense with high melting points due to metallic bonding using (n−1)d and ns electrons; Zn, Cd, Hg are soft and low-melting. Radii fall then level off across a series; lanthanoid contraction makes 4d and 5d radii nearly equal. Ionisation enthalpies rise irregularly.

Irregular ionisation enthalpies (Cr, Cu, Mn, Zn)
remember: High IE₂: Cr (3d⁵), Cu (3d¹⁰); high IE₃: Mn (3d⁵), Zn (3d¹⁰)
Density increases from Ti to Cu

Don't link Zr/Hf similarity to actinoid contraction

topics.title: Oxidation states and stability of higher oxidation states

learn.hook: Manganese can show every oxidation state from +2 to +7. Potassium permanganate's purple and manganese dioxide's black are just two of its many faces.
points: Transition elements show variable oxidation states because the (n−1)d and ns electrons are close in energy, so different numbers can be lost or shared; oxidation states usually differ by one.
The number of oxidation states is greatest in the middle of the 3d series: Mn shows +2 to +7. At the ends there are few: Sc mainly +3, Zn only +2.
Highest oxidation states rise up to Mn (Sc +3, Ti +4, V +5, Cr +6, Mn +7) and then fall. Low oxidation states (0, +1) appear in complexes with π-acceptor ligands like CO, e.g. Ni(CO)₄ and Fe(CO)₅.
Fluorine and oxygen stabilise high oxidation states. Oxygen does it better because it can form multiple bonds to the metal: Mn's highest fluoride is MnF₄ but its highest oxide is Mn₂O₇.

Halides: Cu(II) halides exist except the iodide, because Cu²⁺ oxidises I⁻: 2Cu²⁺ + 4I⁻ → Cu₂I₂ + I₂. In water, Cu⁺ disproportionates (2Cu⁺ → Cu²⁺ + Cu) because Cu²⁺ has a much more negative hydration enthalpy.

example.q: Find the oxidation state of Mn in KMnO₄, K₂MnO₄ and MnO₂.

learn.reallife: The Mn in the MnO₂ of a dry cell (+4) and in KMnO₄ used to disinfect village wells in India (+7) shows how one element can play many redox roles.

Mn shows every state from +2 to +7.
Answer: Manganese

quiz.q: Why is the highest oxidation state of a metal often found in its oxide rather than its fluoride?
options: Oxygen is more electronegative than fluorine
Oxygen can form multiple bonds with the metal
Fluorine cannot form bonds with metals
quiz.explain: Multiple M=O bonding lets oxygen stabilise very high oxidation states, e.g. Mn₂O₇ versus MnF₄.

So oxides reach higher states: Mn₂O₇ (+7) vs MnF₄ (+4).

options: Cu²⁺ oxidises I⁻ to I₂ and is reduced to Cu(I)
Iodine is too small to bond with copper
quiz.explain: 2Cu²⁺ + 4I⁻ → Cu₂I₂ + I₂: iodide is a good reducing agent.
steps: Cu²⁺ is an oxidising agent and I⁻ a good reducing agent.
2Cu²⁺ + 4I⁻ → Cu₂I₂ + I₂, so CuI₂ cannot exist.
Answer: Cu²⁺ oxidises I⁻ to I₂ and is reduced to Cu(I)

options: It disproportionates to Cu²⁺ and Cu because Cu²⁺ has a much more negative hydration enthalpy
It is oxidised by water to Cu³⁺
It has an incomplete d subshell
quiz.explain: The large hydration energy of the smaller, more highly charged Cu²⁺ more than compensates for the second ionisation enthalpy.
steps: In water, 2Cu⁺ → Cu²⁺ + Cu.
Cu²⁺ has a much more negative hydration enthalpy, which outweighs its second ionisation enthalpy.
Answer: It disproportionates to Cu²⁺ and Cu because Cu²⁺ has a much more negative hydration enthalpy
quiz.mistake: Ignores hydration enthalpy

quiz.explain: CO is a neutral ligand, so nickel is in the zero oxidation state.
quiz.mistake: Treats CO as carrying a charge
steps: CO is neutral
Answer: 0

quiz.q: Which is the highest oxidation state shown by vanadium?
quiz.explain: V has 3d³ 4s², so it can use all five electrons, as in V₂O₅.
steps: V = [Ar] 3d³ 4s²: five outer electrons.
Using all five gives +5, as in V₂O₅.
Answer: +5

A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Because the two sets of electrons are close in energy, varying numbers can be used in bonding.

R: (n−1)d and ns orbitals are very close in energy. True.
Close energies let varying numbers of electrons be used, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A

teach.praise: Chirp! Mn's 3d and 4s electrons are close in energy, so it can use 2 up to all 7 of them!

Oxygen stabilises high states better than fluorine via multiple bonds. CuI₂ does not exist and Cu⁺ disproportionates in water.

learn.hook: Most 3d metals fizz in dilute acid, but copper sits calmly in it. The answer lies in a positive standard electrode potential and the energy accounting behind it.
points: E°(M²⁺/M) is generally negative across the 3d series (e.g. Mn −1.18, Fe −0.44, Ni −0.25, Zn −0.76 V), so these metals liberate H₂ from dilute acids.

Copper is unique with E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V: its high enthalpy of atomisation and ionisation enthalpies are not balanced by its hydration enthalpy, so it does not liberate H₂ from acids (only oxidising acids like HNO₃ react).
Values for Mn, Ni and Zn are more negative than the general trend: Mn²⁺ (d⁵) and Zn²⁺ (d¹⁰) are extra stable, and Ni²⁺ has a very negative hydration enthalpy.

E°(M³⁺/M²⁺): Mn³⁺/Mn²⁺ = +1.57 V and Co³⁺/Co²⁺ = +1.97 V are high, so Mn³⁺ and Co³⁺ are strong oxidising agents. The comparatively low value for Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ (+0.77 V) reflects the stability of Fe³⁺ (d⁵). Cr³⁺/Cr²⁺ = −0.41 V, so Cr²⁺ is a strong reducing agent (it becomes stable d³).
Chemical reactivity: apart from copper, 3d metals are fairly reactive and are oxidised by 1 M H⁺, although some (like Ti and V) are passive due to protective oxide films.

example.q: Cr²⁺ and Mn³⁺ are both d⁴. Why is Cr²⁺ reducing while Mn³⁺ is oxidising?
steps: Cr²⁺ (d⁴) → Cr³⁺ (d³): loses an electron to reach the stable half-filled t₂g³ arrangement — acts as a reducing agent
Mn³⁺ (d⁴) → Mn²⁺ (d⁵): gains an electron to reach the extra-stable half-filled d⁵ — acts as an oxidising agent
This matches E°: Cr³⁺/Cr²⁺ −0.41 V, Mn³⁺/Mn²⁺ +1.57 V
example.answer: Cr²⁺ is oxidised to stable d³; Mn³⁺ is reduced to stable d⁵

learn.reallife: Copper does not liberate hydrogen from dilute non-oxidising acids, but in air sour foods slowly attack it; that is why traditional copper and brass cookware in Indian kitchens is lined with tin (kalai) before acidic dishes are cooked in it.

quiz.q: Why does copper not liberate hydrogen from dilute HCl?
options: Copper has a very negative E°
Copper forms a protective oxide in HCl
quiz.explain: A positive reduction potential means Cu is a weaker reducing agent than H₂, so it cannot reduce H⁺.
steps: E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V is positive, above H⁺/H₂ (0.00 V).
So copper is a weaker reducing agent than H₂ and cannot reduce H⁺.
Answer: E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) is positive (+0.34 V)

quiz.q: What is the main reason for the positive E°(Cu²⁺/Cu)?
options: Cu has a very low enthalpy of atomisation
Cu²⁺ is not hydrated in water
High enthalpy of atomisation and ionisation of Cu are not balanced by its hydration enthalpy
quiz.explain: Turning solid Cu into hydrated Cu²⁺ costs more energy than hydration returns.
steps: Forming Cu²⁺(aq) from Cu(s) needs atomisation and ionisation energy.
For Cu these are high and not balanced by its hydration enthalpy, so E° is positive.
Answer: High enthalpy of atomisation and ionisation of Cu are not balanced by its hydration enthalpy

quiz.q: Why is Mn³⁺ a strong oxidising agent?
options: It readily loses an electron to form d³
It has a full d¹⁰ configuration
It readily gains an electron to form the stable d⁵ Mn²⁺
quiz.explain: E°(Mn³⁺/Mn²⁺) = +1.57 V: reduction to half-filled d⁵ Mn²⁺ is highly favourable.
steps: E°(Mn³⁺/Mn²⁺) = +1.57 V is high.
Mn³⁺ (d⁴) gains an electron to form stable half-filled d⁵ Mn²⁺, so it oxidises others.
Answer: It readily gains an electron to form the stable d⁵ Mn²⁺
quiz.mistake: Confuses oxidising with reducing behaviour

quiz.q: Why is Cr²⁺ a strong reducing agent?
options: It is reduced to Cr metal easily
It is oxidised to Cr³⁺, which has a stable t₂g³ (d³) configuration
quiz.explain: E°(Cr³⁺/Cr²⁺) = −0.41 V; Cr²⁺ gives up an electron to become stable Cr³⁺.
steps: Cr²⁺ (d⁴) loses an electron to form stable Cr³⁺ (t₂g³, d³), so it is a reducing agent.
Answer: It is oxidised to Cr³⁺, which has a stable t₂g³ (d³) configuration
quiz.mistake: Thinks d⁴ ions always behave the same

quiz.q: Why is E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) comparatively low among the M³⁺/M²⁺ couples of the 3d series?
options: Iron does not form a +3 ion
Fe³⁺ has the extra-stable d⁵ configuration
quiz.explain: Because Fe³⁺ (d⁵) is stable, it is less eager to be reduced, so the potential is lower than for Mn or Co.
steps: Fe³⁺ is d⁵, extra stable.
It is less eager to be reduced, so E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) = +0.77 V is comparatively low.
Answer: Fe³⁺ has the extra-stable d⁵ configuration
quiz.mistake: Writes the wrong d-count for Fe³⁺

quiz.q: Which ion is the strongest oxidising agent in aqueous solution? E°: Co³⁺/Co²⁺ +1.97 V, Mn³⁺/Mn²⁺ +1.57 V, Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ +0.77 V, Cr³⁺/Cr²⁺ −0.41 V.
quiz.explain: The highest reduction potential (+1.97 V) means Co³⁺ is most easily reduced.
steps: Strongest oxidising agent = highest reduction potential.
Co³⁺/Co²⁺ +1.97 V is highest.
Answer: Co³⁺
quiz.mistake: Picks the most negative value

quiz.q: Why is E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) more negative than expected from the general trend?
options: Zinc has a high enthalpy of atomisation
Zn²⁺ has a half-filled d subshell
Zn²⁺ has a stable, completely filled 3d¹⁰ configuration
quiz.explain: The stability of d¹⁰ Zn²⁺ makes oxidation of Zn especially favourable.
steps: Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰, completely filled and stable.
This makes oxidation of Zn especially favourable, giving a more negative E°.
Answer: Zn²⁺ has a stable, completely filled 3d¹⁰ configuration
quiz.mistake: Confuses full and half-filled stability

quiz.q: Assertion (A): E°(Mn²⁺/Mn) is more negative than expected from the trend across the 3d series. Reason (R): Mn²⁺ has a stable half-filled d⁵ configuration.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A

learn.hook: Copper sulphate crystals are blue, potassium permanganate is purple and zinc sulphate is white. Count the unpaired d electrons and much of the mystery melts away.
points: Substances with unpaired electrons are paramagnetic (attracted by a magnetic field); those with all electrons paired are diamagnetic (weakly repelled).
Spin-only magnetic moment: μ = √[n(n + 2)] BM, where n is the number of unpaired electrons. n = 1 → 1.73, 2 → 2.83, 3 → 3.87, 4 → 4.90, 5 → 5.92 BM.
In a complex or hydrated ion, the d orbitals split into groups of different energy. An electron absorbs visible light to jump between them (a d–d transition), and we see the complementary colour.

Ions with d⁰ or d¹⁰ configurations have no d–d transitions and are colourless in water: Sc³⁺, Ti⁴⁺, Cu⁺ and Zn²⁺. Coloured examples: Ti³⁺ purple, V³⁺ green, Cr³⁺ violet, Mn²⁺ pink, Fe²⁺ green, Fe³⁺ yellow, Co²⁺ pink, Ni²⁺ green, Cu²⁺ blue.

topics.title: Complexes, catalysts, interstitial compounds and alloys

learn.hook: The urea made in Indian fertiliser plants starts with ammonia from the iron-catalysed Haber process, and sulphuric acid plants depend on vanadium pentoxide. Transition metals are chemistry's matchmakers.
points: Transition metals form many complexes, e.g. [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻, [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻, [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ and [PtCl₄]²⁻, because their ions are small, highly charged and have vacant d orbitals of suitable energy to accept lone pairs from ligands.

They are good catalysts because they can show multiple oxidation states, form complexes with reactants, and (as solids) adsorb reactants on their surface. Examples: V₂O₅ in the Contact process (SO₂ → SO₃), finely divided Fe in the Haber process, Ni in hydrogenation of oils.
Fe³⁺ catalyses 2I⁻ + S₂O₈²⁻ → I₂ + 2SO₄²⁻ via 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂ and then 2Fe²⁺ + S₂O₈²⁻ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2SO₄²⁻.

Interstitial compounds form when small atoms (H, C, N) are trapped in the metal lattice, e.g. TiC, Mn₄N, Fe₃H, VH₀.₅₆, TiH₁.₇. They are usually non-stoichiometric, have higher melting points than the pure metals, are very hard, retain metallic conductivity and are chemically inert.
Alloys form readily because transition metals have similar atomic radii (within about 15%), so one can replace another in the lattice: steels with Cr, V, W, Mo, Mn; brass (Cu + Zn); bronze (Cu + Sn).

example.q: Explain how Fe³⁺ catalyses the reaction between iodide and persulphate ions.

learn.hook: The orange crystals used in old breath-analyser tests and as a primary standard in volumetric analysis are potassium dichromate. Turn the solution alkaline and it switches to yellow chromate.
points: Oxides: the higher the oxidation state, the more acidic the oxide. Mn₂O₇ (+7, a covalent green oil) and CrO₃ (+6) are acidic; V₂O₅ is amphoteric though mainly acidic; Cr₂O₃ is amphoteric; CrO and MnO are basic.

Preparation of K₂Cr₂O₇ from chromite ore: 4FeCr₂O₄ + 8Na₂CO₃ + 7O₂ → 8Na₂CrO₄ + 2Fe₂O₃ + 8CO₂ (fusion in air). Acidify: 2Na₂CrO₄ + 2H⁺ → Na₂Cr₂O₇ + 2Na⁺ + H₂O. Then Na₂Cr₂O₇ + 2KCl → K₂Cr₂O₇ + 2NaCl (K₂Cr₂O₇ is less soluble and crystallises as orange crystals).
Chromate and dichromate interconvert with pH: 2CrO₄²⁻ (yellow) + 2H⁺ ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻ (orange) + H₂O; Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 2OH⁻ → 2CrO₄²⁻ + H₂O.
Structures: chromate is tetrahedral; dichromate is two tetrahedra sharing one corner, with a Cr–O–Cr bond angle of 126°.

In acid, dichromate is a strong oxidant: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O (E° = 1.33 V). It oxidises I⁻ to I₂, Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺, H₂S to S and Sn²⁺ to Sn⁴⁺: e.g. Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6Fe²⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O. K₂Cr₂O₇ is used as a primary standard in volumetric analysis.

Add: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6I⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3I₂ + 7H₂O

learn.hook: A pinch of 'lal dawa' turns a bucket of water pink and kills germs. That's potassium permanganate, one of the most versatile oxidising agents in the lab.
points: Preparation: fuse MnO₂ (pyrolusite) with KOH and an oxidant (like KNO₃ or air) to form dark green K₂MnO₄: 2MnO₂ + 4KOH + O₂ → 2K₂MnO₄ + 2H₂O. In neutral or acidic solution, manganate disproportionates: 3MnO₄²⁻ + 4H⁺ → 2MnO₄⁻ + MnO₂ + 2H₂O.

Commercially, MnO₂ is fused with alkali and oxidised to manganate (MnO₄²⁻), which is then oxidised electrolytically in alkaline solution to permanganate (MnO₄⁻). In the lab, Mn²⁺ can be oxidised by peroxodisulphate to permanganate.
Structures: both manganate (green, paramagnetic with one unpaired electron) and permanganate (purple, diamagnetic) are tetrahedral.

Acidic medium: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O (E° = 1.52 V). It oxidises I⁻ to I₂, Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺, oxalate to CO₂, H₂S to S, sulphite to sulphate and nitrite to nitrate. Dilute H₂SO₄ (not HCl) is used, since HCl would be oxidised to Cl₂.

Neutral or faintly alkaline medium: MnO₄⁻ + 2H₂O + 3e⁻ → MnO₂ + 4OH⁻. Iodide is oxidised to iodate (2MnO₄⁻ + H₂O + I⁻ → 2MnO₂ + 2OH⁻ + IO₃⁻), thiosulphate to sulphate, and Mn²⁺ to MnO₂ (in the presence of zinc sulphate or zinc oxide).

Reactions in acidic vs neutral/alkaline medium

learn.hook: The flint in a gas lighter and the rare-earth magnets in electric vehicle motors use lanthanoids — and India's Indian Rare Earths Ltd mines them from the monazite sands of Kerala.
points: Lanthanoids are the 14 elements Ce (58) to Lu (71) after lanthanum, filling 4f orbitals. General configuration 4f¹⁻¹⁴ 5d⁰⁻¹ 6s²; all Ln³⁺ ions are 4fⁿ (n = 1 for Ce³⁺ to 14 for Lu³⁺).

Lanthanoid contraction: atomic and ionic radii decrease steadily from La to Lu because 4f electrons shield one another imperfectly, so effective nuclear charge rises. Consequences: 4d and 5d elements of a group have similar radii (Zr/Hf), lanthanoids are hard to separate, and basicity of Ln(OH)₃ decreases from La(OH)₃ to Lu(OH)₃.

+3 is the characteristic oxidation state. Ce⁴⁺ (4f⁰) is a strong oxidant (E°(Ce⁴⁺/Ce³⁺) = +1.74 V) and Tb⁴⁺ (4f⁷) is also an oxidant; Eu²⁺ (4f⁷) and Yb²⁺ (4f¹⁴) are strong reducing agents. Stability comes from empty, half-filled or filled f subshells.

Lanthanoids are silvery-white soft metals that tarnish in air. Early members are about as reactive as calcium. They liberate H₂ from dilute acids, burn in halogens to form halides, react with water to form Ln(OH)₃ and H₂, form carbides (Ln₃C, Ln₂C₃, LnC₂) with carbon at 2773 K, and give LnN with N₂ on heating.

Uses: misch metal (about 95% lanthanoid metal and 5% iron, with traces of S, C, Ca and Al) in magnesium alloys for bullets, shells and lighter flints; mixed oxides as cracking catalysts; some oxides as phosphors.

example.q: Why is Ce⁴⁺ a good oxidising agent while Eu²⁺ is a good reducing agent?
steps: Ce⁴⁺ is 4f⁰ but the common state is +3, so Ce⁴⁺ tends to gain an electron: Ce⁴⁺ + e⁻ → Ce³⁺ (E° = +1.74 V)
Eu²⁺ is 4f⁷ (half-filled) but it tends to reach the common +3 state by losing an electron
Both revert to the characteristic +3 state
example.answer: Ce⁴⁺ is reduced to Ce³⁺; Eu²⁺ is oxidised to Eu³⁺

learn.reallife: Kerala's beach sands contain monazite; IREL processes it for rare earths now needed for the magnets in wind turbines and EV motors under India's clean-energy push.

+2 and +4 occur only when they give f⁰, f⁷ or f¹⁴.
Answer: +3

quiz.q: What is the main cause of lanthanoid contraction?
options: Imperfect shielding of one 4f electron by another
Increase in the number of electron shells
quiz.explain: Diffuse 4f orbitals shield poorly, so effective nuclear charge rises steadily and the size shrinks.
steps: 4f orbitals are diffuse and shield one another imperfectly.
Effective nuclear charge rises steadily, so size shrinks: lanthanoid contraction.
Answer: Imperfect shielding of one 4f electron by another
quiz.mistake: Thinks the nuclear charge decreases

quiz.q: Why is Ce⁴⁺ a strong oxidising agent in aqueous solution?
options: It tends to return to the common +3 state by gaining an electron
quiz.explain: E°(Ce⁴⁺/Ce³⁺) = +1.74 V, so Ce⁴⁺ is readily reduced to Ce³⁺.
steps: The common state of cerium is +3.
Ce⁴⁺ gains an electron to return to Ce³⁺ (E° = +1.74 V), so it is a strong oxidant.
Answer: It tends to return to the common +3 state by gaining an electron
quiz.mistake: Gives the reason for Eu²⁺ instead

quiz.q: Which lanthanoid ion is a strong reducing agent?
quiz.explain: Eu²⁺ (4f⁷) is readily oxidised to the common Eu³⁺ state.
steps: Eu²⁺ (4f⁷) tends to reach the common +3 state.
It loses an electron easily, so it is a strong reducing agent.
Answer: Eu²⁺
quiz.mistake: Picks an ion in a higher oxidation state

quiz.q: How does the basic strength of lanthanoid hydroxides change from La(OH)₃ to Lu(OH)₃?
quiz.explain: Smaller Ln³⁺ ions polarise OH⁻ more and hold it more covalently, so basicity falls.
steps: From La³⁺ to Lu³⁺ the ion gets smaller.
Smaller ions hold OH⁻ more covalently, so basicity decreases.
Answer: It decreases
quiz.mistake: Assumes basic strength increases with atomic number

quiz.q: What is misch metal mainly composed of?
options: About 95% lanthanoid metal and 5% iron, with traces of S, C, Ca and Al
quiz.explain: Misch metal is a lanthanoid-rich alloy used in magnesium alloys for bullets, shells and lighter flints.
steps: Misch metal is a lanthanoid-rich alloy.
It is about 95% lanthanoid metal and 5% iron, with traces of S, C, Ca and Al.
Answer: About 95% lanthanoid metal and 5% iron, with traces of S, C, Ca and Al
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with steel or brass

quiz.q: What is formed when a lanthanoid reacts with water?
quiz.explain: Lanthanoids are reactive metals; they form hydroxides and release hydrogen.
steps: Lanthanoids are reactive metals.
With water they form Ln(OH)₃ and release H₂.
Answer: Ln(OH)₃ and H₂
quiz.mistake: Thinks lanthanoids are unreactive like noble metals

quiz.q: Assertion (A): It is difficult to separate lanthanoids from one another. Reason (R): Due to lanthanoid contraction, their ionic radii and chemical properties are very similar.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Similar size and charge make their chemistry nearly identical, so separation is hard.
steps: A: lanthanoids are hard to separate. True.
R: lanthanoid contraction makes their radii and chemistry very similar. True.
Similar properties make separation hard, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not connect similar size with similar chemistry

quiz.q: What is the general electronic configuration of the lanthanoids?
quiz.explain: Lanthanoids fill the 4f subshell, with 6s² and 0 or 1 electron in 5d. 5f¹⁻¹⁴ 6d⁰⁻¹ 7s² is the actinoid pattern.
steps: Lanthanoids fill the 4f subshell after 6s².
General configuration: 4f¹⁻¹⁴ 5d⁰⁻¹ 6s² (5f…7s² is for actinoids).
Answer: 4f¹⁻¹⁴ 5d⁰⁻¹ 6s²
quiz.mistake: Confuses the 4f lanthanoids with the 5f actinoids or with the d-block

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: 'Why do most lanthanoids show +3, yet cerium shows +4 and europium shows +2?'
teach.praise: Chirp! +3 is typical, but +4 or +2 appear when they give empty, half-filled or full 4f — and those ions are oxidants or reductants!
teach.nudge: You said +3 is common. What f-configurations make +2 and +4 possible?

revise.summary: Lanthanoids (Ce to Lu) fill 4f orbitals: 4f¹⁻¹⁴ 5d⁰⁻¹ 6s². Lanthanoid contraction steadily decreases radii, making 4d/5d radii similar, separation hard and Ln(OH)₃ less basic. +3 is characteristic; Ce⁴⁺ is oxidising and Eu²⁺, Yb²⁺ reducing. Misch metal is a key use.
focus: Cause and consequences of lanthanoid contraction
traps: Don't say basicity increases from La(OH)₃ to Lu(OH)₃
Don't call Eu²⁺ an oxidising agent

learn.hook: Uranium fuels the reactors at Tarapur and Kudankulam, and thorium from Kerala's sands is the heart of India's three-stage nuclear programme. Both are actinoids.
points: Actinoids are the 14 elements Th (90) to Lr (103), filling 5f orbitals. General configuration 5f¹⁻¹⁴ 6d⁰⁻¹ 7s², with irregularities because 5f and 6d are close in energy (Th is 6d² 7s²).
Actinoid contraction (decrease in size across the series) is greater than lanthanoid contraction, because 5f electrons shield even more poorly than 4f electrons.

They show a wider range of oxidation states than lanthanoids, because 5f, 6d and 7s levels are comparable in energy. The maximum rises from +4 (Th) to +5 (Pa), +6 (U) and +7 (Np), then falls in later elements; +3 is common but not as dominant.

All actinoids are radioactive; early members have long half-lives, later ones very short. They are reactive metals, especially when finely divided; HCl attacks all of them, but HNO₃ has little effect owing to a protective oxide layer.

Compared with lanthanoids: actinoids have wider oxidation states, larger contraction, lower ionisation enthalpies (early members), more complex magnetic behaviour and are all radioactive (among lanthanoids only promethium is radioactive).

example.q: Why do actinoids show a larger number of oxidation states than lanthanoids?
steps: In actinoids, 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals have comparable energies
So varying numbers of electrons can take part in bonding
In lanthanoids, 4f is buried deeper and rarely takes part, so +3 dominates

learn.reallife: BARC's Advanced Heavy Water Reactor design is meant to use thorium, and India holds a large share of the world's thorium in its coastal monazite deposits.

Nitric acid has little effect because a protective oxide layer forms

revise.summary: Actinoids (Th to Lr) fill 5f orbitals with irregular configurations (Th is 6d² 7s²). Their contraction is larger than the lanthanoids' because 5f shields more poorly. They show more oxidation states (up to +7 for Np) as 5f, 6d and 7s are close in energy, and all are radioactive.

topics.title: Applications of d- and f-block elements and reasoning on trends

learn.hook: From the steel of the Chenab rail bridge to the TiO₂ that makes paint white, transition metals build modern India. Board exams love asking 'Give reasons' about them too.
points: Iron and steels are the most important construction materials, made by alloying iron with carbon and other transition metals (Cr, Ni, Mn, V, W, Mo).
TiO₂ is used as a white pigment; MnO₂ in dry cells; Zn and Ni/Cd in batteries; Cu, Ag and Au (group 11) are coinage metals.
Catalysts: V₂O₅ (SO₂ → SO₃ in the Contact process), TiCl₄ with Al(CH₃)₃ (Ziegler catalyst) for polythene, iron in the Haber process, nickel in hydrogenation of fats.
AgBr is used in photography because it is light-sensitive.

Typical 'give reasons': high enthalpy of atomisation (unpaired d electrons, strong metallic bonds); variable oxidation states (close ns and (n−1)d energies); coloured ions (d–d transitions); catalytic power (variable oxidation states, complex formation, surface adsorption); Zr/Hf similarity (lanthanoid contraction).

example.q: Give reason: Transition metals and many of their compounds act as good catalysts.
steps: They can show variable oxidation states, forming and breaking unstable intermediates
They can form complexes with reactants
Solid metals provide a large surface for adsorption, increasing reactant concentration and weakening bonds
example.answer: Because of variable oxidation states, complex formation and surface adsorption

learn.reallife: The Chenab rail bridge in Jammu and Kashmir, the world's highest railway arch bridge, uses special steels; TiO₂ pigment made from Kerala's ilmenite sands at Kerala Minerals and Metals Ltd, Chavara, whitens paints across India.

revise.summary: d- and f-block elements are vital: iron and steels for construction, TiO₂ as white pigment, MnO₂ in dry cells, Cu, Ag, Au as coinage metals, catalysts such as V₂O₅, Fe, Ni and the Ziegler catalyst, and AgBr in photography.
remember: TiO₂: white pigment; MnO₂: dry cells; AgBr: photography
V₂O₅: Contact; Fe: Haber; Ni: hydrogenation; TiCl₄ + Al(CH₃)₃: polythene
traps: Don't say iron catalyses the Haber process because it is abundant
